lead: Yield line theory finds the load at which a reinforced concrete slab collapses. At collapse the under-reinforced slab cracks and yields along straight lines, the yield lines, which cut it into flat pieces that rotate like a mechanism. Equating the work done by the load to the work absorbed in the yield lines gives the collapse load. It suits slabs of any shape and support, where tables do not exist. Only a few syllabi teach it.
prereq: You need the moment of resistance of an under-reinforced section and Two-way slabs with various edge conditions.

sections.h3: Yield lines and the moment m

blocks.text: Along a yield line the steel has yielded and the slab rotates at a constant moment m per metre of line, the moment of resistance of the section (kN·m/m). For an under-reinforced section m = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub> (d − 0.42x<sub>u</sub>), with x<sub>u</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub>/(0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b). If the steel per metre is the same both ways (isotropic slab), m is the same for a line in any direction.

items: Yield lines are straight and end at a slab boundary or meet other yield lines.
A supported edge is an axis of rotation for the piece next to it; a column is a point the axis passes through.
A yield line between two pieces passes through the point where their axes of rotation meet.
Sagging yield lines (positive) form in the span, hogging ones (negative) along continuous or fixed edges.

sections.h3: The work equation and the upper bound

blocks.text: Give the mechanism a small deflection δ at its deepest point. External work = Σ w × (area of each piece) × (deflection of its centroid). Internal work = Σ m × (projected length of the yield lines of a piece on its axis) × (its rotation θ). Setting them equal gives w. For a square slab of side L simply supported on all edges, the yield lines are the two diagonals: each of the four triangles has area L²/4, centroid deflection δ/3, rotation θ = δ/(L/2) and projected length L. So w L² δ/3 = 4 × m × L × 2δ/L = 8mδ, and w<sub>u</sub> = 24m/L².

Every possible mechanism gives a load at or above the true collapse load: the method is an upper bound. A wrong pattern overestimates the strength and is unsafe, so try the possible patterns (or vary the pattern dimension) and take the smallest load. Elastic coefficient methods such as Table 26 are lower bound methods and err on the safe side.

examples.question: A 4 m × 4 m slab, simply supported on all four edges, has 10 mm bars @ 150 mm both ways at an average d = 100 mm. M20, Fe415. Find m and the collapse load. Then find the collapse load of a 4 m × 6 m slab with the same steel.
steps: Rectangle: the pattern has a ridge along the middle of the long direction and corner lines meeting it at a distance b from each short edge. Trying b (m): 1.00 → 22.08; 1.50 → 19.06; 2.00 → 18.02; 2.38 → 17.84; 3.00 → 18.22 kN/m².
The smallest is at b ≈ 2.38 m: w<sub>u</sub> = 17.84 kN/m². The closed form 24m/(l<sub>x</sub>²(√(3 + a²) − a)²) with a = l<sub>x</sub>/l<sub>y</sub> = 0.667 gives the same, 17.84 kN/m².
examples.answer: m = 16.82 kN·m/m; collapse loads 25.23 kN/m² (square) and 17.84 kN/m² (4 m × 6 m). A guess of b = 1.0 m would have claimed 22.08 kN/m², 24 % too high.

traps: Taking the largest load from several patterns. The method is an upper bound: the smallest load governs.

Using the rotation of only one piece across a diagonal yield line and the true line length. Either use relative rotation 2√2δ/L with length L/√2, or projected length L with each piece's own rotation 2δ/L: both give 8mδ.
Mixing units: m in kN·m/m, spans in m, w in kN/m².
Treating the collapse load as a service load. It is the factored (ultimate) load; deflection and cracking are checked separately.

quiz.a: A line along which the slab has yielded in bending and rotates at a constant moment m per metre.

quiz.q: Why is yield line theory called an upper bound method?
quiz.a: Any valid mechanism gives a collapse load equal to or higher than the true one, so the lowest load over all mechanisms is the answer.

quiz.q: A square slab, 5 m side, simply supported, has m = 20 kN·m/m. Find the collapse load.
With the same m = 16.82 kN·m/m, what is the collapse load of a 5 m square simply supported slab?
For the square slab a student uses the rotation of one triangle, 2δ/L, with the true diagonal length L/√2. What load results, and is the error safe?
quiz.a: Internal work becomes 4 × m × (L/√2) × 2δ/L = 4√2 mδ instead of 8mδ, so w = 12√2 m/L² ≈ 0.71 × 24m/L². It understates the collapse load by 29 %: safe, but the mechanics are wrong and the slab is over-designed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Yield line design is used for slabs with openings, odd shapes and point loads, and for checking existing slabs before a change of use. Its partner, the strip method, gives lower bound designs. Search for "yield line analysis of slabs" and "Hillerborg strip method".

figure.caption: The square slab fails along its diagonals at 25.23 kN/m². For the 6 m × 4 m slab the pattern depends on b; the trials give 22.08 down to 17.84 kN/m² at b = 2.38 m, the lowest, which is the collapse load.
